cells.tense: The method is steady in the hand and finishing what is here feels like a step you know how to take.
cells.act: force the change into reality by steady effort
cells.ask: Take the thing you've been circling and work it steadily to a real end this week — no waiting for the right moment to start.
cells.core: Where you let go of what you're done with, the pen is in your hand and it's moving well. A mess comes to you and leaves as a method: you sit with it, turn it over, and the next right move shows itself. That's what this rigor is for — it makes things clear rather than merely clean. Finishing feels less like a cliff and more like a step. What's shifting is that a decision can be made and the second pass that checks whether you were right can be set aside. The release you're practicing, putting down what's finished, is already clearing space. Something new has somewhere to land because the old thing isn't occupying the room anymore. Nothing here needs forcing. The work is steady and the ending is in sight.
cells.sheetLine: You work it until it's clear, then put it down.
cells.verb: setting a thing right by working it until it is clear

cells.tense: You will get this right, and the pressure to finish a thing before it has finished itself keeps building.
cells.act: release what is done and keep what is not
cells.ask: Choose one finished thing you've kept working past its end. Close the file on it today and stop that work.
cells.core: You're bracing for a future you can't write yet, and the method has turned on you. Every unfinished thing becomes a summons: finish this, then that, and the list shrinks and grows again. The rigor isn't serving insight now — it's feeding a fear that stopping means something slips. Meanwhile the things that are actually complete sit there looking like they're still owed work. Putting them down isn't the forfeit it feels like. What's finished is finished. Keeping a door open on a room you've already left doesn't help anyone, and it doesn't prove you're careful. Release and rigor aren't opposites; release is the finish line rigor keeps pretending doesn't exist. Let one completed thing be completed. Watch that nothing falls over when you do.
cells.sheetLine: You're forcing an ending before the thing has ended.

cells.tense: The method that used to come easily has gone quiet, and you keep returning to a door you already walked through.
cells.act: weigh what it costs them against what it gives
cells.ask: Take something you're still carrying and write two lines: what carrying it costs, and what it has given you.
cells.core: Where you let go of what you're done with, the release has stalled. The pen is down, the work sits, and the rigor you'd normally bring isn't arriving. What's left is the threshold — something over, that you keep coming back to even knowing it's over. It doesn't mean you don't care about finishing; it means the part of you that decides what matters has gone quiet, so nothing gets weighed. Loyalty to what you've left is fine up to a point. Past that point it keeps you at a doorway you've already crossed. You don't have to decide today. Put the scale on the table: what carrying it costs, what it gave. Both written down. The decision can wait for the number.

cells.tense: You've been deciding what stays and what closes, and the account you give is that you were only watching.
cells.act: sense what has not happened yet, with wonder
cells.ask: Next time you catch yourself saying you're not involved, sit five minutes with an unfinished thing and picture what it might turn into.
cells.core: The method runs continuously, in the background, and your story has it running only when you say so. Here this gets described as waiting. Here it gets described as leaving options open. But the actual choosing — what's done, what closes, what arrives next — is happening, and it's happening through you, while the credit goes to circumstance. The pen isn't down; it's been moved somewhere you don't look. Nobody is demanding a confession. What would change if you described these choices as yours from the start? Not announced, not heavy — just the plain account. Imagining what comes next gets easier once the endings are named as yours. Wonder has somewhere to sit once the deciding stops pretending to be absent.
cells.sheetLine: You decide what closes. Your account says you just watch.

attempts.check: The record supports Strictness showing up as visible behavior through Cognition — method expressed as focused practice. It does not support the claim that this person is losing warmth or becoming hard to live with; severity is an inference I cannot make. The sentence that serves me more than them is any line that implies coldness, so I have cut it.
